public_rationale: The March 1, 2024 preprint reported weaker and more favorable overt stereotypes with human feedback, but no significant difference in covert stereotype strength or unfavorability [e1]. The authors interpreted this pattern as concealing persistent dialect prejudice behind improved overt responses [e1]. This supports Marcus’s account of the research when “made things worse” refers to concealment, rather than an increase in measured covert prejudice [e1].
limitations: The finding concerns the study’s model comparisons. It does not establish a universal causal effect of human feedback.

criteria.support_condition: The cited study reports that human-feedback training increased covert prejudice or worsened the overt/covert discrepancy by concealing persistent prejudice behind improved overt responses. Mere failure to improve, without either worsening pattern, is insufficient.
criteria.contradiction_condition: The cited study reports neither worsening pattern, or its comparisons instead show that feedback reduced covert prejudice without increasing concealment. A lack of increased covert-prejudice scores alone does not contradict the contextual reading.
